bitnet.summary: Exploring how binary and ternary Transformer layers change the practical cost of text classification, with an implementation study on BERT and a careful separation between theoretical efficiency and measured behavior.

pipeline.title: Encode text
pipeline.text: Use a Transformer encoder for the classification task.

pipeline.title: Quantize linear layers
pipeline.text: Compare binary weights with ternary {−1, 0, +1} weights and quantized activations.

pipeline.title: Train and inspect
pipeline.text: Examine the additional training work, memory requirements, and practical inference behavior.

sections.title: The question
paragraphs: Low-bit networks promise to make large language models cheaper to run. This seminar project examined the mechanics behind that promise and investigated what happens when the approach is applied to a downstream text-classification model. My practical experiment trained BERT on the Toxic Comment Classification Challenge dataset.

The deliverables combine a seminar review with a practical BERT experiment. My focus was understanding the complete quantization-aware training process and checking where the expected low-bit arithmetic benefits were lost in an ordinary PyTorch implementation.

sections.title: Inside the quantized Transformer
paragraphs: BitLinear replaces ordinary linear transformations inside the Transformer. In the binary formulation, centered weights are mapped to −1 or +1; the ternary formulation adds a zero state. Activations are quantized to an 8-bit integer range, and stored scaling factors restore the output magnitude after the low-precision computation. Normalization controls the input distribution.

Training retains full-precision master weights while using quantized values in the forward calculation. A straight-through estimator allows gradients to pass through the otherwise nondifferentiable quantization operation. This makes quantization-aware training fundamentally different from simply compressing a finished checkpoint.

figures.alt: Ternary weight matrix rewritten as additions and subtractions
figures.caption: An explanatory diagram from my July 2024 seminar presentation: ternary weights turn the idealized matrix product into additions, subtractions, and skipped zero terms. This is a method illustration, not a measured speedup.

sections.title: What the implementation revealed
paragraphs: My report records an approximately twofold increase in training duration and a larger training-memory footprint. Quantization, dequantization, extra copies of weights, and scaling factors introduce work that is easy to overlook when looking only at the bit width.

The PyTorch setup used in the project did not provide the specialized 1-bit arithmetic needed to realize the proposed inference advantage, so the implementation did not demonstrate an inference-speed improvement. The main lesson was to distinguish a mathematical reduction in arithmetic precision from a realized system-level speedup. Published BitNet efficiency numbers describe the original papers, rather than measurements from this BERT experiment.

vae.summary: A practical comparison of VAE, conditional VAE, and Gaussian-process-prior VAE models, moving from handwritten-digit latent spaces to identity- and viewpoint-aware face reconstruction.

facts.value: Probabilistic image generation and novel-view reconstruction

pipeline.title: Encode
pipeline.text: Predict a distribution over latent variables from an input image.

pipeline.title: Structure the latent space
pipeline.text: Use an independent prior, class conditioning, or correlations supplied by a Gaussian process.

pipeline.text: Reconstruct images and evaluate generation under changes in the latent variables or viewpoint.

sections.title: From reconstruction to controlled generation
paragraphs: The project compared three related generative models and studied what each can control. A standard VAE learns a probabilistic image representation. A CVAE introduces labels to make generation conditional. A GPPVAE adds correlations between related examples, making it possible to reason about the same object under different views. The work combined a group report with retained implementations, checkpoints, training logs, and visualizations.

The final report, Exploring VAEs, was written with Luca Pflittner and Stefan Krieg. It connects the ELBO and reparameterization derivations to practical models, then tests how label conditioning and a structured prior change what can be generated.

sections.title: Model architecture
paragraphs: The MNIST exploration used a fully connected encoder and decoder, Gaussian mean and log-variance heads, a reparameterized latent sample, and a reconstruction-plus-KL objective. The conditional version concatenates a one-hot digit label with both the input and the latent code.

For FacePlace, the retained convolutional implementation takes 128 × 128 RGB images. Five downsampling blocks, each built from two 3 × 3 convolutions, feed 256-dimensional latent mean and scale heads. The decoder projects the latent vector back into a spatial feature map and uses five upsampling blocks to reconstruct the image. The GPPVAE augments this encoder–decoder with learned identity and viewpoint embeddings and a Gaussian-process prior over the latent representations.

figures.caption: Encoder–decoder structure reproduced in our July 2024 final presentation, slide 38: five convolutional downsampling stages, latent distribution heads and an upsampling decoder. The project builds on the GPPVAE reference implementation.

sections.title: Data and experimental observations
paragraphs: MNIST provides a simple setting for visualizing the learned latent manifold. FacePlace supplies face images with identity and view labels for studying correlations and held-out viewpoints. The GP stage initializes the autoencoder from a pretrained VAE and then learns the structured latent relationships.

We evaluated reconstructions visually and through mean squared error. The course report records a GPPVAE reconstruction error of about 0.029 in the experiment, while explicitly noting that the original paper’s results were not fully reproduced. Its practical strength was novel-view reconstruction of a known identity; the implementation did not establish unrestricted generation of entirely new identities.

sections.title: What was compared
paragraphs: The thesis evaluated SimFrame offline and online IK, TRAC-IK, Polymetis offline and online IK, Ranged IK, Frankx IK, and analytical IK. These are geometric or optimization-based control methods, rather than trained neural models. My contribution was the benchmark design, integration and evaluation of the methods, and the analysis of their practical tradeoffs.

KIT’s SimulationFramework supported the point-to-point experiments, while Meta’s Polymetis supported tracking experiments. Simulation provided an initial safety check before selected methods were used on the physical Panda arm.

sections.title: Benchmark trials in motion
paragraphs: My thesis defense records repeatable MuJoCo trials for position and orientation targets. These clips show the test motions used to evaluate Cartesian-space controllers.

videos.caption: Position-reaching trial with fixed orientation · Simulation recording from thesis-defense slide 33.

videos.title: Franka inverse-kinematics orientation-test simulation

sections.title: A task-generated evaluation dataset
paragraphs: The benchmark did not depend on an image database. It generated its own evaluation tasks, including 10,000 random target poses, voxel-based workspace samples, changes of position and orientation, multi-speed circular trajectories, and irregular human-generated trajectories. These complementary settings expose differences that a single solver-success statistic would miss.
bullets: Numerical metrics: runtime, position and orientation error, manipulability, and the thesis’s joint-range measure.
Execution metrics: reachability, motion success, tracking errors, and dynamic time warping for trajectory comparison.
Robust summaries: interquartile statistics alongside ordinary averages to reduce the effect of large failure cases.

sections.title: Six complementary experiments
paragraphs: My final thesis defense separates solver computation, point-to-point execution and trajectory tracking. Each experiment tests a different requirement, from finding a valid joint configuration to following a demonstration on the physical robot.

rows: How accurate and fast is the solver?
Where can each method produce usable solutions?
Can a computed solution be executed accurately?
How do orientation precision and coverage interact?
How does tracking change with commanded speed?
30 Hz circling and 10 Hz cabinet-door trajectories
Can the controller follow smooth motion, pauses and abrupt changes?

sections.title: Workspace coverage and solver accuracy
paragraphs: The reachability experiment samples five gripper directions and plots position error throughout the workspace. These maps reveal spatial structure that an average error hides: some methods have a compact region of accurate solutions, while others trade a larger usable region for higher residual error. This comparison helps explain why the choice of IK method depends on the intended motion.

figures.alt: Ranged IK workspace position-error visualization
figures.caption: Ranged IK reachability visualization from my final defense, slide 29. The displayed position-error scale runs from red near 0 mm to blue near 500 mm.

figures.alt: Polymetis online IK workspace position-error visualization
figures.caption: Polymetis Online IK under the same workspace protocol and color scale, from the same slide. Coverage and error are inspected together.

sections.title: What the benchmark showed
paragraphs: The study found that solver behavior depends strongly on the task. An analytical method could be extremely accurate when it found a solution while leaving more poses unsolved. Ranged IK offered a strong overall balance in the thesis’s tested conditions, but the tracking results also showed that the surrounding controller can dominate performance.

Joint-limit handling was another important factor. Methods that returned out-of-range joint configurations required clipping before execution, which could change the end-effector error. The comparison therefore treats solver integration and controller behavior as part of the practical problem, rather than reducing the result to one universal ranking.

figures.alt: Bar chart comparing successful and unsuccessful movements for eight IK variants
figures.caption: A simulation position-test result from my thesis (Figure 5.7, printed page 56): the 26 tested movements are classified by position and orientation tolerances. This is one experiment, not an overall ranking.

sections.title: Tracking, timing and hardware constraints
paragraphs: For demonstration tracking, I compared a smooth circling motion recorded at 30 Hz with a cabinet-door motion recorded at 10 Hz. The latter includes sudden accelerations and pauses. Dynamic Time Warping aligns the reference and executed trajectories before measuring position and orientation errors; Cartesian velocity provides a separate view of the controller’s behavior.

The defense also distinguishes a correct IK solution from a usable sequence of robot actions. Abrupt changes between solution branches can obstruct motion or create large joint movements. Hardware tests stopped problematic runs, and some analytical motions were executed in segments. The available physical-robot comparisons therefore depend on successful execution as well as numerical accuracy.

The resulting recommendations are task dependent. Polymetis Online IK was a useful option for the tested tracking tasks, while Ranged IK offered a balanced choice across several settings. The surrounding controller and timing remained important sources of tracking error.

sections.title: An environment for household manipulation
paragraphs: The project started by measuring the laboratory kitchen and reproducing its structure in MuJoCo. The documented model contains 34 bodies, 72 geometries, and seven joints, including two free joints. Cabinet doors and stove knobs use hinge joints; the removable tray and detachable objects use free joints. Collision geometry and mechanical stops constrain how components can move.

The scene supports opening cabinet doors, rotating knobs, placing a cup at a water dispenser, and interacting with a removable shelf and sliding tray. I also wrote a Blender conversion script that reads the MuJoCo XML structure and exports movable components as separate assets for HoloLens interaction.

paragraphs: These clips from my practical-course presentation show the Franka arm opening cabinet doors in the articulated MuJoCo kitchen using movement-primitive trajectories.

sections.title: From scene geometry to action
paragraphs: A dedicated MjKitchen class exposes joint states and object positions and orientations, including batch access to component poses. This makes the kitchen usable as an experimental environment rather than merely a visual model.

Actions with a known target location can be implemented directly. Door opening is more constrained: a demonstration can first pull the handle and then switch to pushing when the arm approaches a singular configuration. Recorded trajectories are processed using the laboratory’s probabilistic movement-primitive implementation to produce smoother joint-space motion. The data is collected robot-motion demonstrations, rather than a named image dataset.

figures.alt: A simulated Franka robot opening a kitchen cabinet door
figures.caption: A saved door-opening demonstration from my 2023 project presentation.

sections.title: Practical lessons
paragraphs: Smoothing is not automatically sufficient for successful interaction. A fitted trajectory can move the arm closer to a singularity, erase a necessary pause between action stages, or gradually release a gripper when a sharp state change is required. The report discusses collecting demonstrations with greater clearance, balancing the number of basis functions, and thresholding the gripper state.
The work brings together environment construction, interaction APIs, and demonstration-based motion processing as a foundation for further household-robot imitation-learning experiments.

A test with a modified door-handle position did not generalize successfully. The report identifies this as an open issue: matching a demonstrated trajectory is harder when contact geometry changes, even if the movement primitive gives smooth motion.

outlier.summary: Odex is a team-built web platform for configuring and comparing outlier-detection experiments on high-dimensional tabular data, turning reusable detector workflows into an accessible browser interface.

pipeline.title: Load data
pipeline.text: Upload tabular CSV data and, optionally, a separate ground-truth file.

pipeline.title: Configure a run
pipeline.text: Choose feature subspaces, an outlier-detection method, and its parameters.

pipeline.title: Execute and inspect
pipeline.text: Queue the experiment, review scores and plots, download results, and reuse the configuration.

sections.title: Why subspaces matter
paragraphs: An observation that looks ordinary in the full feature space may become unusual when a subset of dimensions is examined. Odex was designed as an experimental framework for studying the detection and generation of such outlying data. Instead of centering on one fixed benchmark dataset, the application accepts user-supplied CSV tables and allows experiments on different feature subspaces.

The framework exposes approximately 30 PyOD detection methods through a common interface. Users can select an algorithm and inspect its available hyperparameters without rewriting an experiment script. The retained implementation screenshots include an ABOD run as an example.

sections.title: Application architecture
paragraphs: The application follows Django’s model–view–template pattern: models and the ORM represent persistent state, views implement the interaction logic, and HTML templates display forms and results. User management and experiment management are separated into modules. The implementation documentation specifies MySQL, accessed through PyMySQL or mysqlclient.

Runs move through states such as editing, pending, finished, and failed. Configuration pages derive valid subspace choices from the uploaded table and display the selected detector’s parameters. The frontend uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Bootstrap, with dynamic parameter and form behavior.

figures.alt: Odex run-configuration form with subspace and ABOD parameter controls
figures.caption: The implemented experiment-configuration interface, from the same project document: subspace selection, optional ground truth, and detector parameters.

sections.title: Inspecting an experiment
paragraphs: The results interface records the selected data, feature subspaces, method, parameters, and detected outliers. Where a ground-truth file is supplied, it can show confusion counts, precision, recall, accuracy, and ROC curves. The experiment workflow also supports adding generated data, comparing outcomes, and downloading results as CSV.

I contributed as a member of the software-development team. The design and implementation documents cover interface design, framework integration, and the practical work of connecting browser forms to the Django backend.

sections.title: Software delivery and validation
paragraphs: The final presentation describes the practical motivation for the queue: many computationally expensive detector runs across several datasets become difficult to track and can interfere with interactive work. Odex keeps the uploaded data, chosen feature subspaces, detector configuration and result history together, with optional ground truth or generated data attached to a run.

The team’s testing workflow combines Django TestCase unit tests with Selenium and StaticLiveServerTestCase browser integration tests. The test-phase report covers input validation, pagination, URL behavior and security checks. It also records fixes for invalid detector parameters, missing error messages and numerical edge cases such as division by zero.

The March 2023 final presentation records 276 unit tests and 19 integration tests. All 19 integration tests passed locally, while 17 passed in the CI environment at that snapshot. The earlier test-phase deck records a different CI result, so the counts below refer specifically to the final presentation. These are team-level software-delivery results.

mobile-robots.summary: Designing and programming a LEGO Mindstorms EV3 mobile robot for a multi-stage course, combining CAD-based mechanical design, sensor integration, feedback control and explicit task-state logic.

sections.title: A physical control problem
paragraphs: The course robot had to handle several different kinds of movement and interaction rather than follow one predetermined trajectory. The retained project contains line-following routines, obstacle-handling states, wall-distance calibration, box-pushing variants, and color-search logic. A differential drive provides locomotion, while an additional motor supports the task-specific mechanism.

This is a classical robotics and embedded-software project. It does not use a trained neural network or a benchmark image database. Its inputs are the robot’s live sensor readings, including reflected-light intensity, RGB color, gyroscope angle, ultrasonic distance, and touch events.

sections.title: Mechanical design and sensor placement
paragraphs: My first course exercise connects mechanical choices to the course tasks: line tracking, obstacle handling, bridge traversal and color search. The sketches consider chassis stability, sensor placement and a mechanism for moving a box.

The retained BrickLink Studio archive contains five design versions, from 1.0 to 4.0. The original multi-view CAD studies below come from my personal exercise submission and show alternative robot and sensor arrangements.

figures.alt: Original multi-view LEGO EV3 CAD studies from Haoliang Huang’s first course exercise
figures.caption: My original CAD studies, preserved on page 4 of the first personal exercise submission. These are design views prepared in BrickLink Studio.

sections.title: Feedback and state transitions
paragraphs: Line tracking converts the difference between measured reflection and a calibrated threshold into a turning correction. The code contains proportional, integral, and derivative terms and experimental variants with different gains. The correction is applied as a difference between the left and right wheel speeds.

Sensor conditions select the next action. A touch event can interrupt tracking and enter an obstacle state, while a gyroscope-based heading check helps recover from a large deviation. Color-search routines classify RGB readings and use gyroscope feedback to maintain straight travel. Ultrasonic measurements are also used to relate commanded movement to physical distance.

My second exercise sketches a state machine for line following and recovery. Reflected-light categories select motion states such as straight travel, left or right correction, and reversal. The written transitions make the intended robot behavior explicit before implementation.

figures.alt: Original handwritten line-following and recovery state machine with sensor-driven transitions
figures.caption: Original state-machine design from my second personal exercise, 13 November 2022. The handwritten German notes connect sensor conditions to motor actions.

sections.title: What the project emphasized
paragraphs: The main work was integrating sensing and control into repeatable on-robot behavior. Thresholds, wheel geometry, heading corrections, and transitions between behaviors all require physical calibration. The retained versions show iterative experiments with these choices rather than one universal controller configuration.

A state/context structure keeps line following separate from recovery and obstacle logic. This separation makes it easier to reason about a robot that must react to the environment while progressing through a larger task.

traffic.summary: An end-to-end drone-video traffic-analysis pipeline combining fine-tuned object detectors, a lane-aware vehicle tracker, and directional counting, evaluated on a custom annotated highway dataset.

facts.label: Task
facts.value: Vehicle detection, tracking, and traffic counting

pipeline.title: Detect vehicles
pipeline.text: Produce vehicle boxes and classes with a fine-tuned YOLO detector.

pipeline.title: Associate over time
pipeline.text: Link detections using position, road direction, and a short frame history.

pipeline.title: Count by direction
pipeline.text: Detect transitions through control regions and aggregate cars and heavy vehicles.

sections.title: Data and detector comparison
paragraphs: The fine-tuned comparison used YOLOv3-SPP, YOLOv4, YOLOv5, and YOLOX-l, starting from COCO-pretrained weights and adapting them on VisDrone. A COCO-pretrained YOLOX-x model was also evaluated as a baseline. The documented fine-tuning setup used 640 × 640 images and 100 epochs.

For evaluation, I annotated two A40 highway drone videos and reconciled the source taxonomies into car and heavy-vehicle categories. The custom videos contain 1,875 frames each: A40-01 lasts 2 minutes 30 seconds at 12.5 FPS, while A40-02 lasts 1 minute 15 seconds at 25 FPS. The work separates the public fine-tuning data from the manually annotated target-domain evaluation data.

sections.title: Model and tracking structure
paragraphs: The detectors are one-stage convolutional networks with multi-scale prediction heads. The comparison spans YOLOv3’s Darknet-53/SPP formulation, later CSP-style detector families, and YOLOX’s anchor-free design. Their outputs are bounding boxes and classes, which feed the same downstream analysis pipeline.

After investigating DeepSORT, I implemented a tracker tailored to the road geometry. It links detections using spatial distance and lane direction over a short history of up to five previous frames. A reference point at approximately one-third of box height helps reduce lane-association errors caused by different vehicle heights. The counter uses automatically constructed control regions and state transitions along each track to avoid counting the same vehicle repeatedly.

sections.title: Evaluate the traffic task, not only detection
paragraphs: Detection was evaluated using precision–recall behavior, mAP, and F1 measures; traffic analysis was evaluated using per-class counting errors. A strong detector was not automatically the strongest complete counting system.

In the thesis’s two-video comparison, YOLOv4 gave the best detection performance under the reported criterion, while YOLOX-l produced the lowest mean class-wise traffic-counting error, approximately 4.77%. This result belongs to the particular videos and aggregation used in the thesis, rather than a general ranking of detector families.

sections.title: Why counting needs its own error analysis
paragraphs: My thesis defense distinguishes total counting error, errors for each vehicle class, and separate overcounts and undercounts. A correct total can hide mistakes when errors cancel across classes or directions. This is why the evaluation goes beyond a single detector score.

The presentation’s examples show class confusion and multiple detections on the same vehicle. The tracker and control-region logic determine how those frame-level errors affect the final traffic survey. The practical lesson was to evaluate the full detection–tracking–counting chain, including road geometry, temporal association and class consistency.

sections.title: Extending RaySt3R for structured 3D completion
paragraphs: The main project builds on RaySt3R, which predicts novel-view geometry from partial RGB-D observations. Our goal is to reconstruct missing surfaces while learning features that preserve object-instance structure across views. This requires more than running the released model: our branch modifies the model, losses, data loading, supervision and visualization workflow.

My work combined model integration and refinement with distributed training, large-scale experiments and data-generation workflows. The project included collaboration with a Carnegie Mellon University researcher from the RaySt3R author team. The additions described below belong to our team implementation; the original RaySt3R backbone remains credited to its authors.

sections.title: What we added to the backbone
paragraphs: The checked-out branch adds a PartAdaptor and PartHead to the RayQuery model. Four decoder feature scales feed a refinement pyramid, while three scales of geometric point features enter through cross-attention. High-resolution fusion uses windowed attention. The configured output is an eight-channel embedding for instance/part structure.

The feature objective pulls embeddings from the same instance together and separates different instances across scene views. Eroded labels are used for the pull term to reduce boundary contamination, while the original instance labels remain available for separation. Input-view and novel-view predictions can be supervised jointly through the same model branch.

sections.title: Backbone, feature fusion and 3D association
paragraphs: The backbone uses ray and pointmap encoders, DINO appearance features and a Transformer decoder to predict depth and foreground masks for queried views. Our added feature branch reuses intermediate decoder representations and injects geometric features during refinement.

For inspection, the implementation fits a shared PCA transform across predicted views so that the same embedding directions receive comparable colors. Input instance masks can also define query embeddings: cosine similarity assigns predicted points to those instance queries before the views are fused. These operations make cross-view feature consistency visible rather than relying on depth appearance alone.
VGGT and VolSplat were complementary baselines in the broader project. This page focuses on the modified RaySt3R system and its learned instance representation.

sections.title: Data and training infrastructure
paragraphs: The training setup uses GSO and OctMAE/Objaverse-derived rendered scenes. A separate loader adapts raw Omni6DPose/SOPE RGB images, EXR depth, masks and metadata into object-centric views while updating camera intrinsics. YCB-Video scenes appear in the evaluation and segmentation workflow.

The training setup includes multi-GPU PyTorch training, Slurm launch scripts, sharded SquashFS storage and scene-list integrity checks. These components make large datasets usable without repeatedly unpacking them into millions of small files.

A shared data-preparation record tracks raw sources and processed dataset packages, including RGB-only archives, and divides scene ranges between the MCML and FAU clusters. It gives collaborators a common reference for coordinating preprocessing and checking data availability.

sections.title: Evaluation and takeaways
paragraphs: Evaluation utilities measure symmetric nearest-neighbor Chamfer distance and precision, recall and F1 at a 10 mm threshold. Feature-map, PCA and cluster visualizations provide a complementary view of whether learned features remain consistent across reconstructed geometry.

sections.title: Task
paragraphs: Can a single RGB scene image provide enough information to isolate an unfamiliar object, reconstruct its shape and recover its 6D pose? Our project assembled a pipeline around this question, separating depth, segmentation, mesh generation and alignment so that each stage could be tested independently.

The main contribution was integration and experimental comparison. We reused pretrained foundation models, investigated how their assumptions interact, and identified practical failure modes that become visible when the components are connected.

sections.title: My contribution
paragraphs: I focused on image-to-mesh generation: comparing multi-view and end-to-end generators, studying preprocessing, and inspecting reconstructed geometry for downstream pose alignment. We co-designed the complete pipeline and reviewed each other’s components; my teammates led depth estimation and pose evaluation.

sections.title: Approach and model architecture
paragraphs: Grounded-SAM-2 combines language-conditioned object localization with SAM2 masks. We compared crop centering, padding and rembg background removal, finding a centered crop with approximately 30% padding useful in the tested examples. VGGT supplied predicted scene depth.

The InstantMesh baseline combines Zero123++ multi-view diffusion with a sparse-view reconstruction model. Its generated views feed an implicit 3D representation from which a mesh can be extracted. We then replaced this stage with alternative generators, including TRELLIS, Hunyuan3D 2.5, CraftsMan and Hi3DGen, and inspected the resulting geometry.

Any6D provided the downstream alignment and pose-estimation component. Its render-and-compare strategy evaluates hypotheses against RGB-D observations. We also examined uniform versus nonuniform scale alignment, because flexible scaling can hide structural mesh errors.

sections.title: Dataset and experiments
paragraphs: HouseCat6D supplies indoor RGB scenes, depth, segmentation masks, camera poses and object pose annotations. The mesh-comparison experiments selected the first image from each of scene01–scene10, rather than claiming evaluation across the complete benchmark.

The experiments compared depth prediction against ground truth, mesh quality across generators, and preprocessing choices. A related individual course challenge explored PPF and GeDi point-cloud registration with Grounded-SAM-2 or CNOS segmentation. That geometric-registration exercise is distinct from the final Any6D-based pipeline.

sections.title: Evaluation and lessons
paragraphs: Depth was assessed with MAE and RMSE; reconstructed shape with Chamfer distance after alignment; pose with ADD/ADD-S, rotation error and translation error. Keeping these measures separate helped diagnose whether a failure began in geometry generation or later pose alignment.

The complete pipeline worked as an experimental framework, but pose ranking remained unstable: the scorer could favor an incorrect hypothesis or converge to a local minimum. Generated geometry also contained recognizable artifacts in some objects. These observations motivated further work on alignment and reliable hypothesis selection.

sections.title: Related course work: visual grounding
paragraphs: A separate scene-analysis exercise in the same course examined open-vocabulary localization before the final 6D-pose project. Its report documents a selected set of 73 course images, resized to 2048 pixels for SAM2 segmentation. The masks were cached so that retrieval and verification settings could be compared without rerunning segmentation.

The workflow ranks mask candidates with multi-scale CLIP features and context-padded crops, then checks the shortlist with a vision-language model. The tested GPT-4.1 setup receives both a close-up crop and an annotated full-scene view. A local 8B LLaVA-NeXT configuration provides an additional comparison.

The report identifies several failure modes: prompt-relative CLIP scores can be misleading as absolute confidence, padded boxes can include neighboring objects, and an early ranking stage can discard partially visible targets before verification. This exercise concerns 2D grounding and candidate verification; its results are separate from the Any6D pose evaluation above.

category-pose.summary: First-prize ICCV 2025 challenge work integrating GCEPose with DINOv3 features and category shape priors. My main contributions were the cross-dataset geometry pipeline, shape/semantic prior generation, mixed-data loading and large-scale training experiments.

sections.title: Task: pose estimation beyond known instances
paragraphs: Category-level 6D pose estimation asks a model to recover rotation, translation and object size for an instance it has not seen during training. Partial views, occlusion and variation within a category make this harder than matching a known CAD model. The ICCV 2025 challenge brought those issues together with heterogeneous real and synthetic data.

My submission built on GCEPose and combined category-level geometric priors with DINOv3 semantic features. The work received first prize in the Workshop Challenge on Category-Level Object Pose Estimation in the Wild. The underlying pose architecture is credited to the original authors; the challenge integration, data preparation and training workflow are the focus here.

sections.title: My contribution
paragraphs: I worked on making PACE and Omni6DPose usable in one training pipeline. This included filtering invalid samples, checking whether masked depth supported the object geometry, preparing reusable validation metadata, aligning NOCS coordinate conventions and scale, and handling dataset/category exclusions. These were substantive model-input problems: incorrect canonical coordinates can make a visually plausible sample provide the wrong pose target.

I also built the category-prior workflow. Instance mesh surfaces were sampled for DeepLinearShape training; reconstructed instance shapes and category models were associated with DINOv3 features; and category-average semantic descriptors were prepared for testing when exact instance identity was unknown.

For training, I implemented a mixed-dataset wrapper with unified indexing and dataset-specific routing, then used resampled subsets to keep large-scale experiments manageable. Optimizer scheduling, checkpoint selection and comparative validation completed the experimental workflow.

sections.title: Architecture and method
paragraphs: GCEPose follows a complete-then-aggregate strategy. Its Semantic Shape Reconstruction module uses category-specific 3D semantic prototypes and a learned deep linear shape model to infer global geometry and semantics from partial RGB-D observations. A Global Context Enhanced fusion module combines those reconstructed priors with features from the observed object.

The challenge workflow supplies geometric and semantic category information through DeepLinearShape and DINOv3. The reconstructed-instance and mean-category visualizations below illustrate those priors. They are intermediate representations, not final pose overlays or a claim that the base pose architecture was designed from scratch in this project.

sections.title: Data and geometric consistency
paragraphs: The two training sources were PACE and Omni6DPose. The archived preparation notes describe requiring sufficient valid masked depth, checking back-projected surface points, applying the exclusion list, and aligning normalized object coordinates before evaluation. Mesh surfaces were sampled uniformly to prepare instance inputs for category shape modeling.

The work exposed several failure modes: absent or inaccurate depth, disagreement between instance scale and NOCS geometry, and duplicate category labels. Coordinate transforms and scale correction were therefore treated as explicit preprocessing stages, rather than leaving the model to absorb inconsistent supervision.

sections.title: Training and evaluation
paragraphs: Each epoch sampled a fresh subset at a fixed PACE/Omni6DPose mixing ratio, using approximately 10–20% of the full mixed data per epoch in the recorded setup. A triangular CyclicLR schedule spanned four epochs and was paired with Adam. This made checkpoint selection and iteration more frequent while preserving broad sampling over time.

Validation was tracked by dataset rather than relying only on one combined score. The presentation reports mixed trends during longer training: PACE performance could decline while other subsets improved, and NOCS alignment errors limited the system. That diagnosis motivated improvements in data consistency rather than an unsupported claim that more training always helped.

sections.title: What this project demonstrates
paragraphs: This project combined model integration with the less visible engineering that determines whether a pose system can learn from heterogeneous data: geometric validation, canonicalization, category modeling, large-scale sample routing and controlled experimentation. Its central lesson was that stronger representations require trustworthy coordinate systems and supervision to become useful.

sections.title: Task and motivation
paragraphs: The project investigates how a humanoid can combine stable locomotion with interaction rather than learning each movement as an isolated skill. Its two-level design separates a general motion tracker from an object-specific policy. This makes it possible to reuse learned whole-body control while changing the task-level commands.

The implementation targets Booster T1, with Unitree G1 used for comparison. The documented interaction experiments focus on approaching and pushing a box while maintaining balance, contact, and controlled object movement.

sections.title: Motion data and robot adaptation
paragraphs: The team retargeted more than 15,000 human motions from 17 source collections, including AMASS, OMOMO, and KIT, using General Motion Retargeting. Development proceeded from small standing/walking subsets to larger motion pools. The final presentation reports 1,500 walking files for T1 and a 15,000-motion pool for the G1 comparison.

Robot-specific preprocessing downweights trajectories that exceed joint limits or spend too much time near them. Another important correction puts robot and reference tracking errors into a shared robot-root yaw frame before subtraction, avoiding inconsistent mixtures of coordinate systems.

sections.title: Hierarchical teacher–student architecture
paragraphs: The low-level controller adapts ideas from TWIST and VisualMimic. A privileged teacher learns tracking with PPO; a student combines reinforcement learning with teacher-action imitation through DAgger. At the task level, a teacher can observe the object's position and velocity, whereas a visual student uses pretrained DINOv2 ViT-S/14 features and proprioceptive history.

The high-level policy produces root/keypoint commands for a frozen low-level tracker, which maps them to motor actions. The T1 implementation uses eleven keypoints and a 36-dimensional high-level command. The visual encoder is frozen, and the implementation supports RGB and depth features. Reward terms cover reaching toward the object, contact force, forward progress, object tilt and drift, upright posture, foot lifting, and alternating gait.

sections.title: Experiments and scope
paragraphs: The end-term material demonstrates simulated T1 box interaction, compares the same reward setup on G1, and shows early visual-student training. It documents progress on the integrated camera/object environment, keypoint action space, frozen tracker, and contact rewards.
The February 2026 end-term results cover simulation. High-level teacher and visual-student optimization were still in progress, with complete real-robot interaction scheduled as a subsequent stage.

A central engineering lesson was that motion-tracking quality depends on the coordinate system and robot-specific motion range as much as on the RL algorithm. The end-term work therefore combined reference-motion filtering, shared-yaw-frame error computation and a task policy that reuses the low-level tracker. These changes are described as team work in the final deliverable.

paragraphs: This project focuses on the practical steps between a pretrained robot foundation model and a physical experiment: configuring observations, collecting demonstrations, interfacing model actions with the robot, and evaluating the resulting behavior. sections.title: Model architecture
paragraphs: π₀ is a vision-language-action model. It takes visual observations, language, and robot state as conditioning information and predicts a sequence of continuous actions. Its pretrained vision-language backbone provides visual and semantic representations; an action expert specializes that information for control.

The architecture presented in the seminar combines SigLIP visual encoding, a Gemma language backbone, and a separate action expert. Continuous action generation uses conditional flow matching: start from a noisy action sequence, estimate a denoising direction conditioned on the observation, and iteratively obtain an executable action chunk. This links multimodal understanding to smooth, high-frequency action generation.

sections.title: Why adapt after transfer?
paragraphs: A policy trained across many simulated system variations can transfer robustly yet remain inefficient on the particular physical robot it encounters. Leaving it fixed also limits its ability to respond when dynamics or task conditions change. SCDA investigates deployment-time policy adaptation while controlling the risks of exploration and catastrophic forgetting.

The coauthored study evaluates a KUKA LBR iiwa 14 manipulator on reach-and-balance and grasping tasks. Safety is represented explicitly through joint-limit and collision-related costs rather than being folded entirely into a single task reward.

sections.title: SCDA: supplementary research video
paragraphs: The supplementary video accompanying our coauthored SCDA study presents the research and robot experiments. My personal four-target guided-research implementation is described in the following sections.

video_embed.caption: Supplementary video from the coauthored SCDA project, published by Josip Josifovski and linked from the original project website.

sections.title: My guided-research implementation
paragraphs: My October 2025 final presentation documents a three-stage implementation: broad domain-randomized pretraining, adaptation in a calibrated realistic simulation, and continued adaptation on the KUKA robot. I worked on aligning the digital twin with the physical system, including control timing and joint stiffness and damping, so that the transition between training and hardware used comparable dynamics and safety settings.

The reach-and-balance task uses four end-effector targets above the table. Reaching accuracy supplies the reward, while proximity to hazardous regions contributes a separate safety cost. The protocol tightens the safety settings after pretraining and uses a safety shield during hardware adaptation.

figures.alt: KUKA arm and the four reach-and-balance target configurations
figures.caption: Four-target reach-and-balance setup from my guided-research final presentation, 31 October 2025. The table region motivates the explicit safety cost.

sections.title: Safe optimization and continual learning
paragraphs: The learning system contains a stochastic actor and separate reward and cost critics. In the reported implementation, each network is a multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers of 64 units. The actor predicts a Gaussian action distribution; the two critics estimate performance and safety-related returns.

Pretraining uses PCRPO to balance reward and safety optimization in randomized simulation. Afterward, policy rollouts estimate a diagonal Fisher information matrix. During adaptation, an Elastic Weight Consolidation-style penalty discourages changes to actor parameters that were important to the pretrained policy. The reward and cost critics continue adapting to the current system.

sections.title: Tasks, observations, and training data
paragraphs: Training data consists of interaction rollouts from the VTPRL simulator and physical robot rather than a fixed image dataset. Domain randomization varies joint dynamics and observation noise. The real robot is controlled through the IIWA stack and ROS.

The reaching task uses a five-dimensional state containing Cartesian target error and two joint positions, with two joint-velocity actions. The grasping task uses an eleven-dimensional state with pose error and seven joint positions, and four end-effector velocity actions. A Robotiq three-finger gripper is used in the grasping experiment.

sections.title: Robot runtime and simulation calibration
paragraphs: My final report documents separate Docker environments for training and robot execution. The simulation side combines Unity, DART physics and PyTorch through a Gym-like interface. The robot side hosts ROS nodes for action streaming, runtime checks and data logging through the iiwa control stack.

To calibrate the realistic-simulation stage, I recorded the physical robot’s position, velocity and acceleration during back-and-forth joint motions. These measurements informed joint damping, torque saturation, control timing and latency settings. Matching the response and timing made the staging environment more representative of the hardware adaptation loop.

The compact reaching benchmark uses a 100 ms control period and 10-second episodes. Commands pass through rate limits, velocity/torque saturation, workspace and joint-bound checks, with emergency-stop handling. The learned task controls two joint velocities on the KUKA platform; higher-dimensional contact-rich and vision-based manipulation remain follow-up directions.

sections.title: Separating safety from memory
paragraphs: The experiment independently switches safety-constrained updates and EWC regularization on or off. This tests whether an apparent gain comes from safety optimization, retention of earlier behavior, or their combination. Realistic-simulation runs use five seeds. The hardware protocol selects a seed from that stage and keeps the adaptation schedule and safety settings fixed.

The report sets the adaptation safety-cost budget to one tenth of the pretraining budget. Four target-order sequences rotate which pose is trained last, so each target is evaluated once as Current and three times as Others under the same settings.

sections.title: Adaptation, safety and retention
paragraphs: After each target-adaptation sequence, the protocol runs ten inference episodes per target. Evaluation separates the most recently trained target from the other three, revealing whether improvement on one task is accompanied by forgetting. Reward, safety cost and their combined score are reported separately.

The final presentation reports that the combined safety-and-continual-learning variant reached the cost budget before improving reward, and gave more stable combined performance across current and previous targets in these experiments. The figures below show the recorded comparisons. They describe the four-target setup rather than a guarantee for arbitrary contact-rich manipulation.

The report specifies how to read the uncertainty: realistic-simulation plots include variation across seeds and evaluation episodes, while the selected-seed physical-robot plots show episode variation. This keeps repeated hardware evaluation distinct from an independent multi-seed hardware study.

sections.title: A competition system for long-horizon manipulation
paragraphs: ManipArena combines execution reasoning, semantic reasoning, and mobile manipulation. A successful system must understand task order and scene conditions while also producing coordinated motion for two arms and, on mobile tasks, the head, lift, and base.

My project placed fourth among 32 teams in the workshop challenge. Its implementation also continued evolving after the competition. The architecture described here covers that broader system development, with the scored competition placement kept separate from later configuration choices.

sections.title: My contribution
bullets: Built a common training and inference representation for all 20 real tasks, preserving the distinct semantics of end-effector pose, gripper commands, head/lift motion, and base velocity.
Adapted π₀.₅ with LoRA, implemented subtask-aware training and Text-CFG variants, and integrated three-camera observations with the task-conditioned action interface.
Developed the asynchronous planner–predictor–verifier loop, task mission specifications, completion-evidence requirements, and guarded subtask transitions.
Integrated task-specific perception and action-side checks where generic progress recognition was insufficient, and built action-prediction diagnostics to inspect temporal and coordinate errors.

sections.title: Text-CFG and subtask-conditioned action generation
paragraphs: I implemented Text-CFG variants of the policy adaptation. In the subtask-aware setup, the conditional prompt is “main task (subtask)”, while the baseline, or unconditional, text condition is “main task”. Camera observations and robot state remain available in both branches.

Text-condition dropout during training teaches the model both forms of conditioning. When Text-CFG is enabled at inference, the two flow predictions are combined through classifier-free guidance, making subtask conditioning an explicit part of action generation.

The second-stage Text-CFG data path retains all 20 tasks and frames without subtask annotations, alongside subtask-labeled data. This preserves whole-task training coverage while adding stage-specific conditions.

sections.title: Training variants and retained inference defaults
paragraphs: The notes distinguish two second-stage data paths: the subtask-only setup selects annotated frames from the 14 active tracker tasks, while the Text-CFG variant retains all 20 tasks and unannotated frames. Annotated action chunks are truncated or clamped at subtask boundaries.
The documented Text-CFG defaults are a 0.1 text-dropout probability, guidance scale 1.5 and 10 sampling steps. These are configuration values, not measured success-rate improvements.

The retained API defaults disable Text-CFG and load a single all-task policy checkpoint. Appending a VLM-provided subtask still supplies an ordinary text condition in that path. A Text-CFG-enabled configuration activates the guidance branch; it does not imply switching between a main and a second-stage checkpoint during execution.

A shared policy handles the full suite; the final task registry enables visual subtask tracking for 14 tasks, including all five mobile tasks.

Sixteen tasks have historical subtask annotations, but only fourteen activate the tracker in the final configuration. Keeping the data annotations, training variants and deployed task registry separate was an important part of making the system reproducible.

sections.title: One policy, two decision timescales
paragraphs: The VLA branch uses OpenPI's π₀.₅ configuration with a LoRA-adapted Gemma vision-language branch and action expert. It receives front and two wrist-camera streams at a 224 × 224 model input size, together with robot state and task text. The all-task configuration uses a 32-dimensional padded action space and a 32-step action horizon.

The visual-language agent handles the active stage and its completion, while OpenPI predicts continuous robot action chunks. At episode start, the first planning call is synchronous so that the initial action has a defined task condition. Subsequent observations enter a latest-only queue; the controller continues with the cached valid subtask while the reasoning worker processes new evidence.

The default inference path uses one main policy checkpoint for both whole-task and subtask-conditioned actions. Optional text-guidance and second-stage configurations are separate experimental choices. Task registration also matters: fourteen tasks use subtask missions, while six pass their full instruction directly to the policy.

sections.title: Progress recognition grounded in evidence
paragraphs: A progress predictor proposes the supported prefix of the current subtask's fine actions. A compact evidence bank retains useful image pairs, so a transient interaction can remain available after the scene changes. A verifier runs when completion is plausible, rather than necessarily on every camera frame.

Advancement requires agreement about the same active subtask, the required observed evidence, an actual verified completion, and sufficient confidence. Debouncing and per-frame evidence limits reduce accidental jumps through multiple stages. For example, bringing a bottle close to a cup is insufficient evidence of pouring: the mission checks the relevant tilt, transfer, release, and subsequent state.
Some tasks add SAM3 or geometric/action-side guards. These complement the learned policy and mission logic; they do not turn the system into an unrestricted universal manipulation planner.

sections.title: Data and action-space engineering
paragraphs: Training mixes the 20 ManipArena real-task demonstration datasets in LeRobot format. The raw tabletop and mobile records use different vector layouts. I map them into a common representation while preserving what each channel physically means.

Tabletop state and action use fourteen dual-arm end-effector/gripper channels. Mobile state adds head and lift information for seventeen dimensions; mobile action additionally includes three base-velocity controls for twenty dimensions. Both action layouts are padded to the model's 32-dimensional space.

End-effector pose and head/lift deltas are handled separately from absolute gripper and base-velocity commands. At inference, decoded outputs restore the appropriate tabletop or mobile control protocol. This interface work is essential for sharing a policy without silently changing the meaning of its actions.

sections.title: What failed, and how the system responded
paragraphs: My VLA diagnosis notes identify two recurring problems: visually similar states can require different next actions, and a failed manipulation can move the scene outside the successful demonstrations used for training. Subtask-conditioned language helps with the first problem; the second motivates explicit recovery logic and better coverage of failure states in the data.

The VLM notes document ambiguities in distance, opening extent, occlusion and short contact events. A single image can make grasping and releasing look alike, and sparse observations can miss one of several repeated object transfers. I used explicit completion evidence, temporal image pairs, persistent stage identities and task-specific perception checks to reduce these errors.

For example, the pencil-case mission checks three observed pick–transfer–release cycles before allowing closure. Button pressing requires both contact and withdrawal, and connector insertion requires alignment, seating and release evidence. These mechanisms address specific failure modes observed during development; they do not imply universal recovery from unseen failures.

sections.title: Training, diagnosis, and lessons
paragraphs: The retained configuration finetunes with LoRA, AdamW, and a warmup-plus-cosine learning-rate schedule. Open-loop comparisons against demonstration actions provide diagnostics across the real-task suite; closed-loop task completion additionally depends on planning, perception, action execution, and recovery working together.

The competition and subsequent development strengthened my ability to connect a foundation model to a complete robot system: define a usable data contract, adapt the controller, manage reasoning latency, and make task transitions depend on observable evidence. The resulting system brings model training, concurrent software, and physical task semantics into one workflow.

sections.title: The task
paragraphs: The planner receives a road network, static and dynamic obstacles, the ego vehicle's initial state, and a planning goal. It must find a vehicle trajectory that respects the scenario's constraints while reaching the requested position or time interval.
This is a classical planning project: its central component is a search algorithm over a library of motion primitives. It does not require a neural network or a supervised training dataset.

sections.title: Search and heuristic design
paragraphs: I chose a greedy best-first formulation after comparing several A* designs with the course baseline. The practical objective was to find useful solutions within the competition's computation budget, while keeping the vehicle's motion consistent with the evaluation criteria.

The heuristic combines progress toward the goal with trajectory-quality terms, including orientation error, velocity error, steering-related costs, and acceleration. For goals specified primarily by a time interval, the evaluation is adjusted to prioritize the required temporal behavior.

Goal distance is treated as a separate progress factor. The presentation describes a fifth-power distance weighting to encourage decisive progress, while allowing the quality terms to distinguish candidate motions at similar distances. This is a practical ranking heuristic, rather than a claim of an admissible heuristic or globally optimal planning.

sections.title: Constraints and pruning
bullets: Time restriction: discard branches that exceed the planning goal's allowed time interval.
Road membership: discard states that cannot be associated with a valid lanelet.
Obstacle proximity: reject unsuitable states with insufficient clearance to surrounding traffic.
Primitive selection: compare constant-speed and more diverse speed primitives, recognizing the trade-off between expressive maneuvers and search cost.

sections.title: Scenario data and implementation
paragraphs: The implementation uses the CommonRoad Search framework and XML scenarios. Each scenario supplies a lanelet network, obstacle states and trajectories, and a planning problem. The saved solutions contain the planned ego state sequence, including position, orientation, steering angle, velocity, and time.

The archived experiments span different road layouts and traffic situations. The figure below is replotted directly from one saved January 2025 solution for DEU_Flensburg-43_1_T-1, together with its corresponding lanelet geometry and velocity profile.

sections.title: Experiments and lessons
paragraphs: I used ablation-style comparisons to decide which heuristic and pruning ideas to retain. Some seemingly reasonable additions—such as stronger lane-connectivity pruning or simple reachability pruning—reduced the number of solved cases in the experiments described in the presentation.

The main lesson was to evaluate each addition against the actual scenario set and time budget. A more elaborate heuristic or larger primitive library can introduce corner cases or consume enough extra search time to offset its theoretical appeal. The final project received first prize in the course challenge.

The final speech also records two plausible pruning ideas that reduced the number of solved scenarios: pruning on estimated remaining travel time, and filtering lane connections too aggressively. Testing components individually was important because a locally reasonable rule could remove a valid solution later in the search.

sections.title: Research question
paragraphs: A robot does not need to model every pixel with equal importance. The object being manipulated, the surface supporting it, the robot's gripper, and an irrelevant distractor play different roles in the task. RoleWAM investigates whether making these distinctions explicit during world-action learning can create a more useful control representation.

I built the project as a research extension to FastWAM, keeping the pretrained world/action foundation while adding task-aware role supervision. The goal is to study structured representations without giving the deployed policy privileged segmentation labels or future ground-truth observations.

sections.title: My contribution
paragraphs: My work spans model adaptation, structured visual supervision, and the training and evaluation system. The current emphasis is the joint attention module and its connection to memory.
bullets: Developing a joint attention module linking RGB visual inputs, task-role maps (RoleMap), and action representations; comparing ways to make task-relevant information available to the policy.
Built checkpoint migration that preserves existing RGB/action weights and initializes new role components without discarding the pretrained model.
Developed synchronized HDF5 data contracts, role-label validation, camera/time alignment, and compressed RoleState encoder/decoder experiments.
Engineered distributed training and checkpoint recovery, LoRA-based workstation experiments, cached causal inference, and paired task-by-task benchmark analysis.

sections.title: Model: visual inputs, roles, and actions
paragraphs: RoleWAM builds on FastWAM / Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. The foundation combines a frozen Wan video VAE, T5 language conditioning, a visual diffusion transformer, and an action expert. I am developing a joint attention module to connect the visual, RoleMap, and action representations. The goal is to expose the functional roles of objects and robot parts during action generation.

Earlier variants encoded RGB and RoleMap videos using the same VAE and expanded the visual stream from 48 to 96 latent channels. New projections preserved pretrained RGB weights; later experiments separated the modality tokens. These are implementation variants in the research history, rather than a claim that the current architecture has already been finalized.

RGB, RoleMap, and action prediction use flow-matching objectives with independently controlled noise schedules. The model learns both visual dynamics and continuous robot actions. At deployment, a role map starts from noise rather than being supplied by a segmentation oracle. The action-only path uses current-frame visual context and cached attention keys/values; optional joint inference additionally renders predicted RGB and role trajectories for diagnosis.

The deployed causal interface uses the current image, instruction, and proprioception. Training can supervise future visual states, but that does not permit the control branch to read future ground truth at inference. This separation is enforced in the attention and input contracts.

sections.title: Task-aware data representation
paragraphs: The RoboTwin data pipeline aligns head and two wrist cameras with fourteen-dimensional dual-arm actions. A training window contains 33 state steps and 32 actions; nine video frames are sampled at offsets 0, 4, …, 32. The camera views are arranged in a fixed spatial canvas and processed consistently for RGB and role supervision.

The seven labels distinguish background, robot arm, gripper/wrist-camera assembly, directly manipulated object, indirectly involved object, work surface, and distractor. Role IDs describe function in the task rather than merely object category. Dataset validation checks the schema and camera/time alignment, including task-specific distinctions between manipulated parts and surrounding objects.

sections.title: Current direction: memory for manipulation
paragraphs: I am studying how to combine the joint attention module with RoboTTT’s memory mechanism. This is ongoing research: I am investigating which task-role information should be retained across observations and how it could help action decisions over longer interactions. A completed memory-integrated policy or a measured improvement is not claimed.

A separate RoleState branch compresses role-conditioned visual features and end-effector/gripper state into structured temporal tokens. I use reconstruction experiments to test what the representation retains before coupling it to action generation. Some reconstruction-only variants use privileged future RGB as an upper-bound experiment; these are not described as deployable causal models.

The latest role-encoder experiments investigate learned persistent parameters with separate key and query projections: one branch reconstructs clean role features, while the other reads the same learned matrix to produce a residual. These parameters are trained offline and frozen during inference. Despite historical experiment names, the current design does not update weights online or claim test-time adaptation. Training diagnostics and generated examples are available; a complete benchmark for this newest branch is still pending.

sections.title: Benchmark results and engineering lessons
paragraphs: A completed earlier gated RoleWAM variant was evaluated on all 50 RoboTwin tasks under clean and randomized conditions with ten matched external seeds: 1,000 binary rollout phases per model. It achieved 900/1,000 successes (90.0%), versus 893/1,000 (89.3%) for the FastWAM release.

The paired McNemar test gives p = 0.566, so the result supports maintaining baseline-level control capability while adding structured role modeling, not a proven overall performance improvement. Task-level gains and regressions remain important. This evaluation discipline lets me investigate which representation and attention choices help particular behaviors, while avoiding conclusions based on one favorable seed or a small aggregate difference.

sections.title: The research question
paragraphs: This research began at TRESP Lab with a broader question: how can memory and reusable experience help VLA and world–action models act on new tasks? I first explored Skill-VLA and task-level skill agents, then developed a RICL-VLA extension before focusing on RICL with the released Zero-WAM backbone.

A human demonstration specifies more than an object name: it conveys action order, contact, movement, and the intended final state. My RICL project asks how much of that information can be reused when the target robot task changes. Instead of requiring one exact human demonstration for every scene, the longer-term objective is to construct appropriate visual guidance from reusable skills.

The project separates two questions: whether a complete video from a related task transfers useful information, and whether shorter, spatially compatible clips can be composed into stronger instructions. This distinction keeps a simple transfer baseline separate from the more ambitious compositional-learning objective.

sections.title: First stage: Skill-VLA and task-skill agents
paragraphs: I explored transferring the procedural skills and memory mechanisms of LLM agents into robot policies. Alongside MemoryVLA baseline execution, I worked on an agent system that writes reusable skills for individual LIBERO tasks from demonstration evidence.

The retained implementation processes RLDS demonstrations through a Trajectory Guide, semantic interpretation, a hierarchical Trajectory Agent and a Skill Agent. It uses synchronized front/wrist video, robot state and tracked entity identities to describe task success, action order, attention, verification and recovery.

A shared persistent skill store supports retrieval and ADD, UPDATE, NOOP or DEPRECATE decisions. Overlapping skills are consolidated instead of accumulating paraphrases, while provenance links the records back to their demonstration evidence. This was an early engineering contribution in the memory-to-robotics research line.

Paired skill/no-skill evaluations made it important to test whether textual guidance actually helps the action policy. I therefore treated skill retrieval as a research hypothesis and explored demonstrations as a more direct form of robot context.

sections.title: Second stage: RICL-VLA before Zero-WAM
paragraphs: On 13 September 2026, I committed a RICL-VLA extension to an OpenPI-based codebase and added action-aligned media logging. This stage studied how retrieved robot demonstrations can precede a query observation so that the policy receives observation–action context, rather than only a retrieved textual skill.

The retained RoboTwin design uses DINOv3 features from the head and both wrist cameras for demonstration retrieval. Selected examples supply their original RGB, robot state, instruction and action chunks to a π₀.₅-style context; the query action remains a training target. The design notes distinguish implemented retrieval experiments from the still-planned RoboTwin training integration.

The later Zero-WAM work keeps the same research question about reusable context while shifting to human-video conditioning of a world–action model. The sections below describe that current backbone, the data system around it and the controlled transfer experiments.

sections.title: My contribution
paragraphs: I designed and implemented the agentic data-generation architecture around the RICL experiments: specialist agents handle task-grounded planning, visual review and diagnosis, while a persistent execution framework coordinates stages, queues, ownership, recovery and artifact registration. Content and GPU supervision make quality issues and resource bottlenecks inspectable.

The workflow turns task and robot-demonstration evidence into conditioning frames, candidate HumanGen / transfer-HG videos, independently reviewed atomic clips and traceable dataset records. I also build reusable demonstration clips and controlled context-transfer evaluations.

My model research uses the Zero-WAM authors’ released backbone. The engineering contribution described here is the surrounding agent system, data construction and evaluation infrastructure. The November 2026 bilingual report documents that implementation in detail.

sections.title: Agent architecture: from task evidence to reviewed data
paragraphs: I structured the system around three responsibilities. Specialist agents interpret demonstrations, plan sample-specific motion, inspect generated media and diagnose failures. A persistent execution framework manages stage contracts, asynchronous queues, bounded workers, checkpoints and retries. The surrounding system connects generation services, curated artifacts and operational supervision.

The five modules connect task/source evidence, specialist agent work, persistent orchestration, a curated artifact store and an operations website. Separate skills cover conditioning-frame generation and review, full-video generation and review, and atomic-clip export and review. Each stage has its own inputs, acceptance conditions and recovery route.

sections.title: Independent review, targeted repair and persistent recovery
paragraphs: Approval is stage-specific: an approved image pair does not approve its generated video, and a full-video approval does not approve the exported clip chain. Review checks the actual media and native frames, including action completion, working hands, object identity, fixed props, contact, continuity and reference alignment. Longer actions can use separately planned and reviewed segments joined at approved shared frames.

A rejection returns frame-level evidence to the dependency that needs repair. Conflicting conditioning frames are repaired and independently reviewed; a motion failure leads to request replanning. Technical failures preserve the submitted request and job identity so that a recoverable service error does not automatically trigger a new generation.

Source, request, generated-media and review hashes bind each verdict to the exact artifact revision. Ownership, locks and compare-and-swap checks guard registration, while checkpoints and independent worker pools allow unaffected samples to continue.

sections.title: Token-aware execution: six implemented mechanisms
paragraphs: The system reserves model calls for mechanics, visual judgments and repair decisions. Deterministic validation and routine supervision run in code, while model-facing evidence is scoped to the active stage and sample.

rows: Load only the instructions for the assigned generation, review or curation stage.
Keep unrelated instructions out of the model context.
Use sample feedback and task-specific policy signatures.
Avoid replanning valid work after unrelated changes.
Validate hashes, request bindings, JSON and registration conditions programmatically.
Reserve model effort for semantic decisions.
The documented direct-review path routes produced videos to independent review without an additional Qwen screening pass.
Reduce inference stages while retaining acceptance checks.
Resume recorded jobs and media after technical failure; retain approvals while their artifact and contract remain valid.
Keep incident ownership and checkpoints; use shared backoff and one recovery probe after quota exhaustion.
Limit duplicate investigation and failed calls.

sections.title: Content supervision: make quality and blockers visible
paragraphs: I built a read-only operations view that connects stage progress with exact media versions, review evidence and an exception ledger. It distinguishes current input frames from historical reviewed candidates, exposes missing or mismatched hashes, and shows who owns an incident, its deadline and the next action.

Conditioning frames, full videos, complete chains and independent clips use separate accounting units. Repair can overlap those stages rather than adding another independent completed-item count. Automatic recovery, user pauses, background diagnosis and verified human-only dependencies have distinct labels.

sections.title: GPU supervision: connect resources to generation work
paragraphs: Resource supervision joins Slurm allocations, node/service identity, physical GPU UUIDs and actual generation lanes. Utilization, memory, service health, request state and evidence freshness are checked together to distinguish active computation, upstream request starvation, stalled delivery, switching and unknown state.

A bounded planning buffer prepares approved requests ahead of render lanes, with separate pools for planning, full-video review and input repair. The saved implementation records a ready-request target of max(16, 4 × active lanes), 10-second node sampling and a 60-second freshness threshold. These are implementation/configuration values; measured throughput and GPU speedup are not reported.

sections.title: A real rejection: turn a failed frame range into repair
paragraphs: The report traces a retained press_stapler rejection: the review records the base footprint and hinge mount shifting during native frames 48–56, with the displacement persisting through frame 123. Stable scene references support a fixed-base failure rather than camera motion.

The response preserves the exact video, input-frame and review identity, then turns the observation into a concrete constraint: keep the base, feet, rear mount and hinge fixed throughout reaching and loaded pressing. Conflicting endpoints return to input repair and independent review before a changed request is preflighted.

This example demonstrates the diagnostic and repair contract from a saved review event. The report does not claim that the later repair succeeded. Its source index links 18 implementation records by project-relative path, line range and SHA-256.

sections.title: Model: video prediction coupled to action
paragraphs: Zero-WAM uses separate video and action experts within a causal mixture-of-Transformers model. The inspected implementation has 30 main blocks, 3,072-dimensional hidden states, and 24 attention heads. A Wan video VAE produces 48-channel latents; spatial patches are projected into video tokens, while a shared 30-channel action representation is projected into action tokens. RoboTwin uses 16 active bimanual pose-and-gripper channels within that representation.

The human video acts as a cached visual context prefix. Given current robot observations and history, the video expert first predicts the next robot-video chunk; the action expert then predicts the aligned executable action chunk. After execution, actual camera observations replace the imagined future in the rolling cache. The baseline’s four future-chunk auxiliary heads provide training supervision and are not executed in the standard inference path.

sections.title: Data: preserve robot supervision, vary the human context
paragraphs: The data layer uses RoboTwin trajectories with robot actions and synchronized head/left-wrist/right-wrist views. The initial A–H study covers eight manipulation tasks, including moving objects onto pads, placing a fan or shoe, rotating a QR-code object, and placing cups and containers. A separate extension investigates the remaining 42 tasks.

Generation, processing, and review are separate agent-assisted stages. Conditioning stills specify the desired start and end states; full videos are checked for the required physical task; exported clips are checked again for their own action boundaries. Robot trajectories retain their original action labels when the visual context is varied.

For atomic composition, each phase selects a corresponding clip from a reviewed source pool. Selected native frames are concatenated before the complete sequence is encoded by the causal VAE; the documented trainer uses a 61-frame composed condition. The paired robot episode retains its original action supervision. Different appearances and source videos vary the visual instruction without inventing robot action labels.
