sections.title: Grid–Goal: compatibility beyond visual similarity
paragraphs: Grid–Goal maps the visible tabletop through a homography into a 3 × 3 coordinate system, using the object’s actual support footprint. GRAB matches the starting cell; PLACE matches the destination cell and task-specific final orientation. MOVE first prioritizes matching endpoints, then permits compatible relative displacements with a direction difference up to 45° and a distance ratio from 0.5 to 2. Horizontal reflection transforms the media and spatial labels together.

This is explicit geometry-and-task-conditioned source selection, rather than a demonstrated learned embedding-retrieval system. The action vocabulary also distinguishes grasping, supported placement, free release, opening, pressing, striking, holding, and handover. Source timing, video hashes, object attributes, and stage-state conditions make the resulting recipes inspectable.

sections.title: Current progress and next experiments
paragraphs: The data audits include 400 training and 160 evaluation scenes in the eight-task study, plus 169 proposed robot action segments from representative demonstrations of the remaining 42 tasks. Candidate availability and reviewed data coverage are tracked separately from robot rollout success. Conditioning images, full videos, and exported clips have separate acceptance stages.

The confirmed exact-grid, final-orientation, and mirror policy still needs a verified integration step in the frozen training selector before a new controlled post-training comparison. Further experiments target reverse-order and mismatched-context controls, stronger held-out-task evaluation, and execution-time clip switching. The aim is to test whether the model follows the composed task specification, rather than merely behaving plausibly.

sections.title: Problem and research direction
paragraphs: A dynamic manipulation policy must reason about objects that move while the robot is observing and acting. Images and language alone do not expose a persistent, explicit representation of which surface points belong to the target or how those points move over time. D4rtVLA explores whether a 4D reconstruction-and-tracking model can supply that missing structure.

The main idea was to adapt and train OpenD4RT beyond reconstruction: predict the future features of important objects in a world-model-like way, then make those features available to the VLA policy for action generation. This predictive objective was the central research direction, not only an offline feature-extraction pipeline.

The working hypothesis is to connect task-relevant object motion features to action generation without replacing the pretrained VLA policy. This remains a research question: an implemented conditioning path and lower errors in a small pilot do not by themselves establish better robot task success.

sections.title: My contribution
paragraphs: I adapted and trained the OpenD4RT-based future key-object feature predictor and investigated its interface with a VLA action generator. Later, I borrowed the instruction-grounding idea from InstructSAM to build InstructD4RT, with the intention of combining it with D4rtVLA.

I developed the integration around the existing DynamicVLA and OpenD4RT models: instruction-conditioned object/mask preparation, accepted-feature sidecars, action-time alignment, multi-view and object-role embeddings, batch-local token padding, and the attention adapter. I also built reproducible dataset subsets, normalization and split checks, paired ablation tools, and visual tracking diagnostics.

A substantial part of the work was defining reliable interfaces between perception and control. Missing or rejected masks must not silently become valid conditioning tokens; source objects, destinations and candidate sources must retain distinct identities; and the same sampled point must stay aligned across pixel coordinates, decoder features and future 3D pseudo-labels.

sections.title: Architecture: 4D features inside a flow-matching policy
paragraphs: The project had two related development stages: future key-object feature prediction using an adapted OpenD4RT model, and policy-side conditioning experiments using a DynamicVLA adapter. The offline sidecar implementation described below is one prototype path; it should not be confused with a completed online future-prediction policy.

The policy retains DynamicVLA’s flow-matching action generator. A 16-layer action expert alternates eight joint self-attention layers with eight cross-attention layers. It predicts a 16-step action chunk, each step containing translation, rotation and gripper commands.

In the offline adapter prototype, OpenD4RT decoder features have 1,280 channels. A shared learned projection, view embedding and role embedding turn them into policy tokens; each cross-attention layer has its own key/value projections. Action query t attends only to the object-point features aligned with that future step, rather than a flattened memory of every future time. A negative initial attention bias keeps the new memory nearly closed at initialization.

The extra features enter the existing cross-attention memory alongside visual, language and robot-state features. They do not create an additional action-attention block. OpenD4RT and segmentation are run offline to prepare detached sidecars, while the policy learns the adapter and action-conditioning path. The stored 3D trajectories are pseudo-labels, not ground-truth robot action supervision.

sections.title: Datasets and reproducible experiments
paragraphs: The prototype uses DOM dynamic-manipulation data and an extended DOM-Plus workflow. I prepared a 2,080-episode DOM subset with 1,664 training, 208 validation and 208 test episodes, consistent reindexing and training-only normalization. Its per-source-chunk split is an IID diagnostic split, not evidence of unseen-task generalization.

A later DOM-Plus setup uses a frozen 80-episode generation-complete snapshot with a task-stratified 64/8/8 assignment. Every raw frame remains a policy sample: frames without accepted guidance take the baseline path. Paired training shares each sample batch and flow-matching noise/time draw across both conditions, which isolates the effect of feature injection more carefully.

sections.title: What the experiments show
paragraphs: Tracking and action generation are assessed separately. Saved YCBInEOAT and HO-3D diagnostics compare predicted object-pixel tracks with corresponding ground truth; they are evaluation of the tracking component, not robot rollouts. Offline policy evaluation excludes padded action steps and reports overall, translation, rotation and gripper L1/MSE.

Results were mixed. In one archived 31/4/4-episode train/validation/test comparison, guidance slightly improved validation action L1 but worsened held-out test action L1. Earlier smaller pilots therefore cannot support a broad improvement claim. Stricter accepted-mask schemas also superseded historical feature sets, making data-version consistency part of the evaluation problem.

sections.title: InstructD4RT and the decision to stop
paragraphs: The later InstructD4RT branch borrowed from InstructSAM to make key-object grounding depend on the instruction. It was intended to provide task-relevant information for the D4rtVLA pipeline. I stopped the direction after finding that InstructD4RT did not generalize sufficiently. The project is therefore a discontinued research prototype, not an active project awaiting deployment.

There were also engineering and evaluation limits: the offline feature pipeline could use future frames from prerecorded clips, streaming inference was not completed, and the retained ablations did not establish a consistent held-out action-prediction advantage. The useful outcome was a clearer understanding of the grounding and generalization requirements for connecting 4D perception to robot action.

This work followed the ManipArena competition within the same TUM research setting. In September 2026, I moved to RoleWAM, investigating task-role representations and joint attention rather than continuing this prototype.

sections.title: The problem: reasoning that survives execution
paragraphs: This is part of my student research assistant work at TUM’s Chair of Cyber-Physical Systems, starting in October 2026, under Youran Wang and Prof. Matthias Althoff. The current agent uses GPT-6.1; archived release-specific studies below include earlier model and configuration choices.

A driving agent has to reconcile route progress, interaction with other vehicles, feasible vehicle dynamics, and a goal with spatial and temporal constraints. A plausible verbal plan is only one part of that problem: it must produce an executable next motion and respond when the traffic changes.

This project investigates a hierarchy in which a language agent chooses strategies and interprets difficult interactions, while numerical planners and native validation handle trajectories and physical execution. The experiments use CommonRoad tasks with live SUMO traffic, so surrounding vehicles evolve in response to the simulation rather than simply following a hidden prerecorded future.

sections.title: My contribution
bullets: Built the agent–environment integration: persistent sessions, structured MCP tools, planning feedback, reference-path interfaces, and explicit action/state receipts.
Developed the decision contracts between high-level reasoning, planner choice, traffic-policy labels, candidate ranking, forward prediction, and bounded automatic execution.
Implemented versioned experimental orchestration, immutable source/input manifests, per-attempt records, independent execution audits, and fresh-initial-state retests after repairs.
Built replay and diagnosis tooling that ties visible vehicle motion to candidate scores, selected trajectories, warnings, strategy changes, and recorded outcomes.
Alongside the planner, developing a Transformer with a logistic-hazard decoder to predict time to traffic-rule violations, with multi-seed validation and feature ablations.

sections.title: Architecture and control boundaries
paragraphs: The language model operates through a constrained tool interface. It can select available planning algorithms, adjust permitted objective or sampling parameters, reason about route/reference choices, and manage interaction policies. It does not directly invent steering commands or advance an unchecked trajectory.

The backend combines reactive planning with rule-based or sampled continuation candidates. It regenerates and validates motion using the current measured state. Candidate generation, ranking, forecasting, and execution are distinct stages, which makes it possible to locate a failure in the appropriate component instead of attributing every problem to the agent prompt.

In the selected-forecast development revision, the configured original objective ranks candidates first. Only the selected trajectory retains its complete native prefix and receives any missing tail needed for a three-second ego forecast. That forecast is compared with traffic occupancy in matching time intervals; constructing an extra long rollout for every candidate is not used as a substitute ranking rule.

Its v0.6.0 architecture includes a section-scoring strategy, several numerical planning options, fallback trajectories and a failure-memory path for difficult road geometry.

The presentation reports 143/143 scenes passed and includes the Augsburg-13_1 and Jena-14_4 replays below. sections.title: Causal prediction and bounded delegation
paragraphs: SPOT/SONIA supplies set-based traffic predictions from current measured actors and the public map. The system distinguishes observed positions, possible future occupancy, and checked motion prefixes. Missing forecast coverage is reported explicitly, with actors still represented by their observed identity and state.

A vehicle's wait label describes a traffic-policy relationship; it is separate from the ego vehicle's actual decision to slow, roll, stop, or approach a conflict area. Physical timing and trajectory checks still determine which movement can execute. These distinctions are important in merging, ordinary car following, and crossing traffic.

The agent can delegate a bounded interval of automatic execution, but the world is rechecked at each 0.1-second step. New hazards, stale state tokens, tracking problems, or the absence of a checked continuation return control with structured evidence. The forward-only studies disable physical rollback and replay, so an unfavorable state cannot be erased during a scored episode.

sections.title: Data, experiments, and results
paragraphs: The task data consists of road networks, vehicle initial states, reactive traffic, and CommonRoad planning goals. It is an evaluation environment rather than a dataset used to train a new end-to-end driving network. Each campaign records the source version, inputs, model configuration, budget, and every attempt.

Two completed evaluation snapshots illustrate the work's scale and the importance of release-specific reporting. The later campaign used a different language-agent/configuration and several separately frozen repair revisions.

bullets: Strict success requires the native goal and validity checks, successful termination, and the independent execution/forecast audit—not merely visual progress toward the target.
Planning noncompletion, actual contact, infrastructure faults, and numerical trajectory cost are recorded separately. Results from different releases are not pooled into a best-case success rate.
The simulator pauses during language-model decisions. These studies evaluate closed-loop behavior and tooling, rather than demonstrating real-time on-road response latency.

sections.title: Current research and engineering focus
paragraphs: Development continues on traffic-policy reasoning, forecast completeness, timing-aware interaction, planner recovery from the current state, and reliable model/tool transport. The published selected-forecast engineering revision has its own component and tool-loading validation; it does not inherit a full-suite result from an older release.

The central capability developed here is connecting an uncertain reasoning system to a stateful physical simulator through explicit contracts, useful feedback, and reproducible experiments. Native CommonRoad, SUMO, planner, and SPOT/SONIA components remain credited foundations; my work is the agentic integration and the execution/evaluation machinery around them.

sections.title: Forthcoming paper
paragraphs: Predictive Monitoring of Traffic Rules Using Survival Analysis — a forthcoming coauthored paper on predicting when surrounding vehicles may violate traffic rules. The selected figures below show the method, neural architecture and a highway driving example.

figures.alt: Observed traffic scene, trajectory history, road network and traffic rule feed a neural violation-time predictor and risk-aware driving response
figures.caption: Method overview from our forthcoming paper: traffic histories, road context and formalized rules inform a predicted distribution of the first violation time.

sections.title: Predict time, not only a violation label
paragraphs: A safety monitor can check whether a traffic rule is already violated. Prediction asks a different question: given the recent motion and scene, when is a violation likely to happen? Event-time modeling also needs to account for censored examples, where no violation is observed within the available interval.

This work is part of my TUM CPS HiWi role and complements the CommonRoad agentic-planning project. The neural predictor and the numerical execution checks are distinct components; this page does not imply that every experiment is already integrated into the driving agent.

sections.title: My contribution
bullets: Designed and refined the neural-network architecture, from grouped vehicle, rule-robustness and road-context encoders to temporal modeling and event-time decoding.
Implemented and tested model variants, and compared MLP, GRU and Transformer encoders with Weibull, PMF, DRSA and logistic-hazard alternatives under a shared evaluation protocol.
Designed and ran the hyperparameter-search workflow: balanced orthogonal-array screening, Optuna TPE refinement and confirmation across common random seeds.
Analyzed controlled feature ablations, checkpoint inventories and metric comparisons to explain which inputs and architectural choices supported prediction quality.

sections.title: Transformer and logistic-hazard model
paragraphs: The model groups the time-varying inputs by their meaning: logical robustness features and vehicle dynamics are encoded with their respective branches, while road segments supply environmental context. A sequence Transformer aggregates the observation history, and a logistic-hazard decoder predicts discrete event-time hazards.

The retained configuration uses an observation history of up to 32 steps, a 64-dimensional Transformer representation, two attention heads, and a road-network encoder. These describe one selected experimental configuration, rather than a universal architecture claim.

figures.alt: Vehicle, robustness and road-segment MLP branches fuse into a sequence encoder with Weibull, PMF or hazard decoders and a survival loss
figures.caption: Neural learning pipeline from our forthcoming paper. Separate feature encoders feed a shared temporal representation; alternative decoders model the distribution of the first violation time. The diagram includes the architecture variants compared in the study.

sections.title: Architecture comparison before tuning
paragraphs: The retained manuscript compares twelve encoder–decoder/objective combinations on five traffic rules and five random seeds. Parameter budgets are kept close to 40 K, so the comparison examines representation and event-time modeling rather than simply increasing network size.

Transformer–Logistic-Hazard has the lowest combined validation rank in that comparison. Transformer–Weibull is close, and other variants lead individual metrics. I therefore compare discrimination, calibration and event-horizon precision together instead of choosing a network from one favorable score.

sections.title: From architecture selection to hyperparameter search
paragraphs: After architecture selection, I searched ten factors covering optimization, regularization, the feature encoders, fusion width, Transformer capacity, attention heads and decoder width. The retained search record uses 567 orthogonal-array configurations for balanced screening and 120 additional Optuna TPE configurations for adaptive refinement.

Screening and refinement use two seeds; the shortlists proceed to confirmation with five common seeds. Checkpoint and configuration selection use validation data, with the independent test split kept out of the search. The selected settings are then held fixed for feature ablations.

The November manuscript snapshot reports a mean validation AUC of 0.9748 ± 0.0013, integrated Brier score of 0.0315 ± 0.0006 and average precision of 0.9505 ± 0.0020 for the selected configuration. Each seed is first averaged across the five rules; the reported variation is the sample standard deviation across the five seeds. These are validation results after tuning.

figures.alt: Architecture comparison, orthogonal-array screening, TPE refinement and five-seed confirmation
figures.caption: Study workflow redrawn from the retained architecture-comparison and search records. The five-rule selection study is separate from the six-rule feature-ablation inventory.

sections.title: Data and validation
paragraphs: The broader workflow uses highD, inD, and MONA traffic data. Temporal histories and traffic-rule robustness features are prepared for event prediction; data-source and rule-specific configurations determine the concrete split and endpoint.

The retained ablation study fixes a selected model configuration and compares six rules under nine feature settings and five common seeds. All 270 selected checkpoints are indexed. AUC, integrated Brier score, and rule-aware average precision are used to inspect discrimination and time-dependent prediction quality.

sections.title: What the feature study supports
paragraphs: In the fixed validation setup, the complete input achieved the highest overall mean composite score. Removing both logical-robustness feature groups produced the largest aggregate loss. This supports the value of rule-related history in that experiment; it does not establish a statistically significant winner for every individual rule.
The study reports seed variation and paired differences. The reported checkpoints and rankings are validation-based, and no independent test evaluation is claimed.

sections.title: From predicted risk to driving response
paragraphs: The coauthored paper also studies how predicted rule-violation risk can inform a driving response. In the highway cut-in example, the predictor estimates the future violation-time distribution and a risk-aware planner decelerates before the unsafe maneuver. The plots compare this replanned response with the recorded run.

sections.title: An educational AR scene with a physical interface
paragraphs: The team project turns nine printed markers into the Sun and eight planets. Looking at a marker reveals its associated 3D model, name and information. Users then rearrange the physical markers to place the planets in their expected order from the Sun.

The application combines classical computer vision, calibrated geometry and interactive graphics. The main engineering challenge is keeping camera images, marker poses, rendered models and game state consistent as markers move or disappear.

sections.title: My contribution
paragraphs: I focused on making game rounds repeatable and keeping the application’s controls aligned with its camera input. My 4–5 July changes covered the following:
bullets: Fixed the restart path by clearing cached planet transforms when beginning a new round, so a previous arrangement does not remain the basis of the next game.
Implemented clearer start, exit and replay transitions, coordinating button text with completion-state handling.
Aligned the window, camera canvas, render viewport and bottom controls with the input image dimensions; updated Windows export and imported-texture settings.

sections.title: Architecture: camera geometry inside an interactive renderer
paragraphs: A native C++ CVCamera component exposes OpenCV capture and marker tracking through Godot’s GDExtension interface. The vision path thresholds the image, finds candidate quadrilaterals and refines their corners. It rectifies each candidate into a small grid, checks the black border and decodes the inner binary pattern across possible rotations.

Four image corners and the marker’s configured physical dimensions feed OpenCV solvePnP. Rotation and translation are converted into a homogeneous pose and then into Godot’s coordinate conventions. The scene maps each recognized ID to its planet model and updates the associated transform and labels.

Camera image dimensions and the projection field of view connect the video background to the virtual camera. The planet assets use adjusted visual scales and labels for an understandable tabletop experience.

sections.title: Game logic, marker visibility and restart behavior
paragraphs: The ordering game uses the tracked planet transforms to compute distances from the Sun and sort the planets. The resulting order is compared with the expected sequence; label colors provide feedback and a completion state controls the success animation.

Marker loss and cached positions must be handled together with game state. My restart fix removes cached transforms at the beginning of a new round, while the start/exit/replay controls determine when completion checks are active. These changes support repeated interaction with the same physical marker set.

paragraphs: Inputs are live or replayed RGB camera frames, nine printed binary markers, and textured 3D planet meshes. The repository includes marker images, Godot scenes, planet assets and several recorded camera sequences for testing tracking and interaction.
